newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Hundreds of Rwandan refugees die in Zaire jungle.
newsitem.headline: Hundreds of Rwandan refugees die in Zaire jungle.

text.p: Hundreds of Rwandan Hutu refugees are dying of disease and hunger near a railway line in the Zairean jungle where aid workers started to bring relief on Friday.
At least 500 Rwandan Hutus have been buried since March 16 at Ubilo, a village 82 km (50 miles) south of Zaire's third city Kisangani, according to Lubinga Nganda, head of a Zairean Red Cross team.
The U.N. refugee agency UNHCR said it found 20 unburied bodies at Ubilo while at a temporary transit camp nearby journalists watched a baby die in its mother's arms.
"There has been a selection. The fittest make it but the unfit die," said Kilian Kleinschmidt, a UNHCR emergency officer.

The U.N. World Food Programme, UNHCR and the Red Cross carried the first trainload of 120 tonnes of food and medicine on Thursday and Friday to the refugees gathered at villages along the railway line running south from Kisangani.
More than a million Hutus fled camps on the Rwandan and Burundian border last October and November at the start of a campaign by rebels fighting the Zairean army.

Around 600,000 returned to Rwanda in November but hundreds of thousands more fled west into the jungle, among them members of the former Rwandan government army (ex-FAR) and extremist Hutu Interahamwe militia who are blamed for the 1994 killing of an estimated 800,000 Rwandan Tutsis and moderate Hutus.
Since then they have set up a series of makeshift camps and fled before the rebel advance in a trek that has hampered relief efforts.
Rebels of the Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) attacked and killed at least 100 of the armed refugees in two incidents last week, according to residents.

The rebels attacked refugees at a point 52 km (32 miles) south of Kisangani on March 20 in an attempt to flush out the armed Rwandans and a two-hour gunbattle ensued, said a health worker who witnessed the incident.

"The ex-FAR and Interahamwe stole everything from us. As you see they stole all of chickens, all of our goats, all of our money. We have nothing," said Atombie Bielo, a local resident. He added the extremists were armed with guns, axes and clubs.
Ubilo villagers said they refused to assist any refugees while the extremists were in the village and hundreds left in the direction of Opala, 150 km (90 miles) southwest of Kisangani.
The refugees lining the railway tracks as the train approached made a pitiful sight.
Emaciated refugees, some almost skeletal, were attempting to walk towards aid at Kisangani but those too weak to start the trek lay dead and dying within the abandoned Ubilo camp.
Red Cross workers dragged one woman to safety after she had fallen into a swamp where she had stayed all night, too weak to pull herself out.
Children scrabbled in the dirt for tree roots or tried to eat bark to assuage their hunger.
At Kisesa village 25 km (16 miles) south of Kisangani up to 35,000 of the stronger refugees gathered, while at Biaro there were around 21,000 with several hundred of the weakest at Ubilo.
The refugees are dying of malaria, dysentry, fatigue and malnutrition, said Bankani Singi, a Zairean Red Cross nurse.
The rebels say the refugees cannot enter Kisangani -- seized on March 15 -- and must eventually go back to Rwanda.
"My name is Louis. I am a schoolteacher from Kigali (the Rwandan capital) and I want to go home to see my daughter," one refugee told Reuters, a sentiment echoed by almost all the refugees.
